extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, litigators, law students, and others interested in patent litigation practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and using claim charts in patent litigation: how to structure charts, the principal types (infringement, invalidity/reference, claim interpretation), and evidentiary/formatting practices used in courts and examiner manuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-column chart structure
rubrics_metrics.description: In each, typically, there are two columns: the left column contains the language of the patent claim under analysis, separated into the successive limitations (e.g., elements or steps, integers, parts) of the claim; the right column contains the information relating to the claim element at its left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a table with the claim broken into discrete limitations on the left and corresponding evidence/analysis on the right. This structure is described as a 'convenient and effective means for analyzing and presenting information regarding a patent claim.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Break claim into successive limitations / integers
rubrics_metrics.description: Break down the claim into suitable integers (i.e. separate parts) in order to explain a case on infringement with reference to specific elements of the alleged infringing product or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UK IPEC Guide and MPEP examples recommend parsing the claim into discrete limitations so each can be addressed individually in the chart; necessary when explaining infringement or invalidity to a court or examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement chart: map each limitation to accused product/process (all elements test)
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringement chart that allegedly shows how the product or process accused of infringement contains each claim element, thereby satisfying the all elements test for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically prepared by the plaintiff/patent owner. For each claim limitation show the corresponding part/feature/step in the accused device or process (and cite evidence, figures, or testimony) so that every limitation is accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chart of references (invalidity): map limitations to prior art passages
rubrics_metrics.description: A chart of references (such earlier patents and magazine articles) that allegedly show the invalidity of the patent because of anticipation or obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically prepared by the defendant/accused infringer. For each claim limitation, identify and quote passages from prior art that teach that limitation; use precise citations (e.g., patent column/line and figure) and split quotations to correspond to specific limitations when appropriate (as in the MPEP example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation chart: cite specification/technical literature for meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim interpretation chart that shows, for each claim element, passages in the patent specification or in technical literature that show the proper meaning or interpretation that should be given to the language of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either party may prepare this chart. For disputed claim terms, collect intrinsic (specification, prosecution history) and extrinsic (technical literature, dictionaries) support and place the relevant citations next to the claim limitation to support the proposed construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligibility (Alice) / abstract-idea mapping charts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim charts may also be used to support an argument that a patent claims ineligible subject matter, such as a law of nature or a conventional business practice. In the right column, the steps or elements of a well known business concept or a way of organizing human activity are listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chart to demonstrate that each claimed step corresponds to routine human activity or a well-known business practice (often illustrating 'do it with a computer' recitation). Courts (e.g., in Alice and Walker Digital v. Google) have used such charts to show claims are directed to abstract ideas and thus ineligible absent an inventive implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include diagrams / figures to show the accused device contains recited elements
rubrics_metrics.description: These charts often contain diagrams of the relevant elements, to show that the device contains the element as recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, annotate or reference figures/diagrams of the accused product or prior art to visually tie claim limitations to physical structures or drawings. Courts and practitioner examples commonly include figures and callouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of quotations and citations (split quotations per limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parse quotations as carefully as needed; split the corresponding quotation into parts corresponding to each limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP example demonstrates splitting a prior-art quotation into parts aligned with claim limitations and providing precise citations (e.g., 'col. 6, lines 2–3; Figure 3'). Precise citation and alignment prevents overbroad or ambiguous mappings and aids examiners/courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness: cover every claim element and corresponding evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Charts should address each claim limitation so a court/examiner can determine whether every claim element is present in the accused product/process or taught by prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to map even one limitation can undermine an infringement or invalidity argument. The Walker Digital example shows courts scrutinize whether every step/limitation is performed or taught when assessing invalidity or preemption concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select chart type for purpose and forum; list of common variants
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three principal types of claim chart (chart of references/invalidity, infringement chart, claim interpretation chart) and other variants: initial or preliminary infringement contentions (PICs); domestic industry (DI) charts for ITC importation actions; expert claim charts; 'parts list' charts used as demonstrative exhibits; claim charts for licensing/settlement negotiations; and design patent charts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the chart variant that matches your objective (e.g., infringement proof, invalidity showing, claim construction support, ITC DI requirement, demonstrative use in trial, licensing discussion). Different forums (district court, ITC, PTO) may have specific content or formatting expectations.
